extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters and art critics (and the periodical press)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive criteria and standards for the creation, exhibition, and critical evaluation of landscape painting (practice, finish, fidelity to nature, and the duties of critics and the press).

rubrics_metrics.name: Works reward familiarity with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Precisely in the degree in which we are familiar with nature, constant in our observation of her, and enlarged in our understanding of her, will [an artist's] works expand before our eyes into glory and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appreciation and interpretation of landscape painting depend on the viewer's knowledge of nature; new insights into nature yield fresh illustration of the artist's principles and confirm his facts. Critics and viewers should approach such works expecting that fuller understanding of nature will reveal previously unseen meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress as cumulative and never sacrificing greater truth
rubrics_metrics.description: He has never sacrificed a greater truth to a less. As he advanced, the previous knowledge or attainment was absorbed in what succeeded, or abandoned only if incompatible, and never abandoned without a gain;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic development should build and absorb prior attainments; progress ought to aim at higher truths rather than discard them for lesser effects. Evaluators should value evidence of cumulative intellectual and technical growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery as consequence of fullness
rubrics_metrics.description: Their mystery is the consequence of their fullness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscurity or indistinctness in mature works may indicate abundance of meaning rather than failure; critics should distinguish obscurity that signals depth from obscurity born of incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material truth (fidelity to nature) as a standard of relative rank
rubrics_metrics.description: That modern artists, as a body, are far more just and full in their views of material things than any landscape painters whose works are extant--but that J. M. W. Turner is the only man who has ever given an entire transcript of the whole system of nature...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fidelity to material facts of nature (truth to nature) is a sound test for comparing painters' relative rank. While not the sole measure of excellence, material truth indicates the depth of observation and technical capacity and should be heavily weighted in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is necessary but not sufficient (beauty and character also count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and beauty, knowledge and imagination, invariably are associated in art; ... truth is indeed a perfect test of the relative rank of painters, though it does not in itself constitute that rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should recognize that technical fidelity must be accompanied by beauty, character, and imagination; excellence requires both factual truth and higher aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity is comparable across subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The fidelity with which they treat either the one or the other, is dependent on those simple powers of sense and intellect which are like and comparable in all... the same delicate sense which perceives the utmost grace of the fibres of a tree, will be equally unerring in tracing the character of cloud;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an artist demonstrates true fidelity in one class of object, similar fidelity should be expected across other subjects; apparent excellence limited to one subject often indicates trickery or shallow skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for sound criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: None are capable of doing this, but those whose principles of judgment are based both on thorough practical knowledge of art, and on broad general views of what is true and right...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should possess practical experience in art-making plus broad principles of truth and right; mere comparisons to past masters (Claude, Poussin) betray lack of practical understanding and are inadequate for modern work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of the press: guide what the public should ask for
rubrics_metrics.description: The press... have not so much to direct the multitude whom to go to, as what to ask for. Their business is not to tell us which is our best painter, but to tell us whether we are making our best painter do his best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical writers should educate the public to value finished, purposeful works and to demand work that furthers artistic development rather than merely pronouncing opinions or invoking classical precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disfavor of unfinished works and rapid production
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most morbid symptoms of the general taste of the present day, is a too great fondness for unfinished works. Brilliancy and rapidity of execution are everywhere sought as the highest good...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasing or encouraging incomplete pictures damages both public taste and artists' development. Critics and dealers should discourage the market that rewards rapid, superficial work and instead promote laboriously finished pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists must finish works perfectly (never let picture leave easel while improvable)
rubrics_metrics.description: It ought to be a rule with every painter never to let a picture leave his easel while it is yet capable of improvement... That only is a complete picture which has both the general wholeness and effect of nature, and the inexhaustible perfection of nature's details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should continuously ask: 'Is my whole right?' and 'Can my details be added to?' A picture is incomplete if any spot can be exhaustively fathomed; completion requires unity of whole effect and fully-realized details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two pitfalls: aiming only at details or only at generals
rubrics_metrics.description: By aiming only at details, he becomes a mechanic; by aiming only at generals, he becomes a trickster: his fall in both cases is sure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice balances detailed fidelity with integrity of general effect. Teachers and critics should identify and correct tendencies toward mechanistic finish or merely flashy generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and encouragement of careful sketches and studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies in chalk, of landscape, should form a part of every Exhibition... We should be heartily glad to see the room which is now devoted to bad drawings... occupied instead, by careful studies for historical pictures; not blots of chiaroscuro, but delicate outlines with the pen or crayon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches and studies (delicate outlines, accurate studies of plants/figures) should be exhibited and valued; they are essential formative work and deserve public and institutional encouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young artists: duty of humble, earnest imitation of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: From young artists, in landscape, nothing ought to be tolerated but simple bona fide imitation of nature... Their duty is neither to choose, nor compose, nor imagine, nor experimentalize; but to be humble and earnest in following the steps of nature, and tracing the finger of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early training must emphasize careful copying from nature, restraint in color (quiet grays and browns), and acceptance of failures as signs of effort. Only after memory and hand are formed should bold invention and vivid color be attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aping masters and premature dexterity
rubrics_metrics.description: They have no business to ape the execution of masters... Nothing is so bad a symptom, in the work of young artists, as too much dexterity of handling; for it is a sign that they are satisfied with their work...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors and critics should discourage mimicry of masterly surface techniques and value honesty of attempt; apparent fluency often indicates superficiality and should be treated as a warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity among greater artists of solemnity and singleness of aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Among our greater artists, the chief want, at the present day, is that of solemnity and definite purpose... We should like to see our artists working out... marked pieces of landscape character... with concentrated powers... definite and pervading thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established artists should pursue concentrated, didactic, or reflective landscapes that aim to impress a single elevated emotion or lesson; avoid facile 'picture-manufacturing' combining minor attractions without a definite end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never repeat oneself; repetition degrades art
rubrics_metrics.description: I would earnestly plead with all our artists, that they should make it a law never to repeat themselves... All repetition is degradation of the art; it reduces it from headwork to handwork;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should seek originality in subject and treatment; quantity achieved by repetition signals diminution of thought and artistic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and realization of subject, light, and details
rubrics_metrics.description: Let then every picture be painted with earnest intention of impressing on the spectator some elevated emotion... Let a real subject be carefully selected... let an effect of light and color be taken which may harmonize with both... let the details of the foreground be separately studied, especially those plants which appear peculiar to the place...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art-making process: choose a genuinely suggestive subject, select an appropriate (recollected) sky/effect of light, study foreground details (local peculiarities), and draw ideal forms from studies so that imagination is minimized to arrangement and connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to imagination: realize then veil
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally, when his picture is thus perfectly realized in all its parts, let him dash as much of it out as he likes; throw, if he will, mist around it--darkness--or dazzling and confused light... the forms, once so laboriously realized, will come out whenever they do occur with a startling and impressive truth...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for combining truth and poetic effect: fully realize forms in study, then employ veiling (mist, obscurity, intensified light) in the finished work to enhance suggestion and imaginative impact without sacrificing underlying fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensibility to color and sensibility to form
rubrics_metrics.description: There are indeed one or two broad distinctions in the nature of the senses,--a sensibility to color, for instance, being very different from a sensibility to form; so that a man may possess one without the other...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and teachers should recognize different types of perceptual talent (color vs. form) and not expect identical strengths from every artist; assessment should account for these distinct faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists should avoid imitating degraded or artificially altered nature
rubrics_metrics.description: They must be careful that it is nature to whom they go--nature in her liberty--not as servant-of-all-work in the hands of the agriculturist... Let them work by the torrent-side, and in the forest shadows; not by purling brooks and under 'tonsile shades.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying nature, prefer wild, unmanipulated scenes over parks, furrowed fields, or horticulturally-altered specimens; ideal forms derive from free, unspoilt nature, not from man-altered or diseased examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press duty regarding great artists (Turner) — treat works as lessons not mere objects of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Our periodical writers... their duty is not to pronounce opinions upon the work of a man who has walked with nature threescore years; but to impress upon the public the respect with which they are to be received... We are not to approach them to be pleased, but to be taught; not to form a judgment, but to receive a lesson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with towering artists, the press should refrain from casual blame or praise and instead present such works as instructive and deserving of solemn reception; encourage these artists to undertake grand, systematic works for national instruction.
